'''''Eucalyptus globulus'' subsp. ''maidenii''''', commonly known as '''Maiden's gum''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus globulus'' subsp. ''maidenii'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_globulus_subsp._maidenii.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=2 June 2020}}</ref> is a subspecies of tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to southeastern Australia. It has mostly smooth bark with some persistent slabs of old bark at the base, juvenile leaves with one glaucous side, lance-shaped adult leaves, flower buds arranged in groups of seven, white flowers and conical, [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicellate]], sometimes [[wikt:glaucous#Adjective|glaucous]] fruit that is more or less square in cross-section[[File:Eucalyptus globulus maidenii buds.jpg|thumb|225px|Flower buds]][[File:Eucalyptus globulus maidenii fruit.jpg|thumb|225px|Fruit]][[File:Eucalyptus maidenii - Kunming Botanical Garden - DSC02953.JPG|thumb|225px|Trunk of tree in [[Kunming Institute of Botany|Kunming Botanical Garden]], China]]

==Description==
''Eucalyptus globulus'' subsp. ''maidenii'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|45-50|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. The bark is mostly smooth, shedding in long strips to leave a white or greyish surface. There is sometimes rough, partially shed bark at the base of the trunk and ribbons of shedding bark in the upper branches. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have stems that are more or less square in cross-section, with a prominent wing on each corner. The juvenile leaves are [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], arranged in opposite pairs, elliptic to egg-shaped, the lower surface covered by a white, waxy bloom, {{cvt|40-110|mm}} long and {{cvt|17-60|mm}} wide. Adult leaves are arranged alternately, the same shade of green on both sides, lance-shaped to curved, {{cvt|120-355|mm}} long and {{cvt|12-40|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|15-37|mm}} long.<ref name="CANBR"/><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Brooker |first1=M. Ian H. |last2=Slee |first2=Andrew V. |title=''Eucalyptus globulus'' subsp. ''maidenii'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/e512acad-0785-4639-bf9f-05b3cb63ded4 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=18 July 2019}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus globulus'' subsp. ''maidenii'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20globulus%20subsp.%20maidenii |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=18 July 2019}}</ref>

The flower buds are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of seven on a flattened [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|8-25|mm}} long, the individual buds on a thickened [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] {{cvt|3-8|mm}} long. Mature buds are club-shaped to pear-shaped, {{cvt|8-11|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-7|mm}} wide with a beaked or flattened [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]] that has a central knob. Flowering has been recorded in March and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, conical, sometimes glaucous [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]], {{cvt|5-8|mm}} long and {{cvt|6-10|mm}} wide with the valves at about rim level.<ref name="CANBR"/><ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="ABRS" />

==Taxonomy and naming==
Maiden's gum was first formally described in 1890 by [[Ferdinand von Mueller]] who gave it the name ''Eucalyptus maidenii'' and published the description in ''[[Linnean Society of New South Wales|Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales]]'' from collections by [[William Baeuerlen|William Bäuerlen]].<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus maidenii''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455630|publisher=APNI|access-date=18 July 2019}}</ref><ref name="F.Muell.">{{cite journal |last1=von Mueller |first1=Ferdinand |title=Notes on a new species of ''Eucalyptus'' (''Eucalyptus maidenii'') from southern New South Wales |journal=Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales |date=1890 |volume=IV (second series) |pages=1020–1022 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/29780#page/1078/mode/1up |access-date=18 July 2019}}</ref> In 1974, [[James Barrie Kirkpatrick]] described four subspecies of ''E. globulus'' and changed the name ''E. maidenii'' to ''E. globulus'' subsp. ''maidenii''.<ref name="K.B.Kirk.">{{cite journal |last1=Kirkpatrick |first1=James Barrie |title=The numerical intraspecific taxonomy of ''Eucalyptus globulus'' Labill. (Myrtaceae) |journal=The Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |date=September 1974 |volume=69 |issue=2 |pages=89–104|doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.1974.tb01618.x }}</ref><ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus globulus'' subsp. ''maidenii''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454635|publisher=APNI|access-date=17 July 2019}}</ref> The epithet ''maidenii'' honours [[Joseph Maiden]].<ref name="CANBR" />

==Distribution and habitat==
This subspecies of ''E. globulus'' grows in forest in mountain valleys, on slopes and ridges in near-coastal ranges of New South Wales south of the [[Shoalhaven River]] and in eastern Victoria near the upper reaches of the [[Genoa River|Genoa]] and [[Cann River]]s.<ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="ABRS" /><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus maidenii'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~maidenii |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=18 July 2019}}</ref>
